title: Morphisms in a left localization are a colimit of ordinary Hom sets
statement: Let $\mathcal C$ be a category, $S$ a multiplicative system, and $Q:\mathcal C\to S^{-1}\mathcal C$ its left localization [def-weil-abstract-derived-category]. For objects $X,Y$ of $\mathcal C$, the canonical map $\varinjlim_{s:X\to I\,\in S}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(Y,I)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{S^{-1}\mathcal C}(Q(Y),Q(X))$ in the usual left-localization orientation is a bijection; equivalently, morphisms in $S^{-1}\mathcal C$ are represented by postcomposition along arrows of $S$ and identified by passage to a later denominator.

source.place: Stacks Tag 0FND, label lemma-pre-derived-adjoint-functors-general, proof line 9515, fifth equality; Categories Tag 05Q0, label categories-remark-left-localization-morphisms-colimit

proof.text: For each denominator s:X⟶I in S, send f:Y⟶I to Q(f)≫Q(s)⁻¹:Q(Y)⟶Q(X). A commuting triangle of denominators gives the same composite after applying Q and cancelling the invertible image of the later denominator, so these maps are compatible with the transition maps. (By Stacks Tag 05Q0 the index category X/S is filtered, so this colimit is a filtered colimit; the argument below does not use this.) They therefore induce the canonical map from the colimit of Hom_C(Y,I) over X/S to Hom_{S⁻¹C}(Q(Y),Q(X)).

source.place: Categories Tag 05Q0, label categories-remark-left-localization-morphisms-colimit, definition of X/S, its filteredness, and displayed formula

proof.text: Given g:Q(Y)⟶Q(X), apply the left-fraction representation statement with its source object instantiated as Y and its target object as X. It supplies f:Y⟶I and s:X⟶I in S with g=Q(f)≫Q(s)⁻¹, so g is the image of the colimit class represented by f at s. Thus the canonical map is surjective.

If f₁:Y⟶I₁ and f₂:Y⟶I₂ over denominators s₁:X⟶I₁ and s₂:X⟶I₂ have equal images, the left-fraction equality statement supplies a common refinement with arrows t₁:I₁⟶J and t₂:I₂⟶J such that s₁≫t₁=s₂≫t₂∈S and f₁≫t₁=f₂≫t₂. This is exactly the relation identifying the two representatives in the colimit over X/S, so the canonical map is injective.

The canonical map is both surjective and injective by the preceding two steps, hence it is a bijection. If S consists only of identity arrows, X/S has the identity denominator as a terminal object and the map reduces to the identity Hom-bijection, as a check on the construction.
